::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
Which modality should this programme pursue? It is the earliest and least
reversible decision in drug development, and everything a modeller later does
— the structural model, the sampling design, the covariates worth testing — is
downstream of it.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**This strand assumes nothing.** If you have arrived from statistics,
mathematics, engineering or software, start here. If you already have a
pharmacology degree, skim `P-01` to `P-05` for vocabulary and go to `P-06`.
:::

## 1. A drug is a molecule that changes what a protein does

Strip away the packaging and a medicine is a chemical that gets into your body,
reaches a particular protein, sticks to it, and changes how that protein
behaves. Everything else — the tablet, the injection, the clinical trial, the
regulatory dossier — exists to make that one event happen reliably, in the right
people, at the right intensity, for the right length of time.

That sentence contains the entire field:

| The requirement | The discipline that owns it |
|---|---|
| **Get in** and survive the journey | Pharmacokinetics — absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion |
| **Reach** the right place | Distribution, tissue penetration, barriers |
| **Stick** to the right protein and not the wrong ones | Pharmacodynamics, selectivity, safety pharmacology |
| **Change** what that protein does, by the right amount | Pharmacodynamics, dose–response |
| **Stop**, eventually, and leave | Metabolism, excretion, duration of effect |

A modeller's job is to put numbers on each row and connect them to a decision.
You cannot do that without knowing what is physically happening, which is what
this strand is for.

## 2. The obstacle course

Follow a tablet. The journey explains most of what pharmacokinetics measures.

**It has to dissolve.** A tablet is a solid. Only dissolved molecules can be
absorbed. Some drugs are so poorly soluble that dissolution — not absorption —
sets the pace of everything downstream.

**It has to survive the stomach.** Gastric acid at roughly pH 1–2 destroys many
molecules outright. Proteins and peptides are digested like food, which is the
single biggest reason insulin and monoclonal antibodies are injected rather than
swallowed.

**It has to cross the gut wall.** The intestinal lining is a sheet of cells, and
crossing it means passing through *two* lipid membranes. Molecules that are too
large, too charged or too water-loving do not get across. Some that do are
immediately pumped back out by efflux transporters — proteins whose day job is
throwing foreign chemicals back into the gut. Which transporters these are, and
when a sponsor is expected to study them, is not left to taste: the
International Transporter Consortium set out the list and the decision trees
(Giacomini et al., Nat Rev Drug Discov 2010,
[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrd3028), free full text; updated by Galetin et
al. 2024, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41573-023-00877-1), free full text).

**It has to survive the liver.** Everything absorbed from the gut travels in the
portal vein straight to the liver *before* reaching the rest of the body. The
liver is an industrial chemical plant for destroying foreign molecules. A drug
can be well absorbed and still have most of the dose demolished on this first
pass — which is why **first-pass metabolism** gets its own lesson (`P-07`).

**It has to be distributed.** What survives enters the bloodstream and is carried
to organs in proportion to their blood supply. On the way, much of it binds to
plasma proteins; bound drug is a passenger, not a participant.

**It has to reach the target.** Which may be inside cells, or behind the
blood–brain barrier, or in a poorly perfused tumour.

**Then it has to leave.** Metabolised by the liver, filtered by the kidney,
excreted in bile — continuously, from the first moment.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Notice that **every step is a rate, not a yes/no**. That is why pharmacology is
quantitative at its foundation, and why differential equations turn out to be
the natural language. The models in `S1` are not imposed on the biology; they
are the biology, written down.
:::

Two of these hurdles can be anticipated rather than discovered. Wu and Benet's
**biopharmaceutics drug disposition classification system** ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11095-004-9004-4))
sorts compounds into four classes on two axes — solubility, and whether
elimination proceeds mainly by metabolism or by excretion of unchanged drug —
and the class then predicts which obstacles will bite. High-solubility,
high-metabolism compounds (class 1) tend to be absorbed completely and to show
little transporter involvement; poorly soluble, highly metabolised compounds
(class 2) are where efflux transporters, food effects and metabolic interactions
concentrate. The classification costs nothing to apply and is available before
any clinical study has run.

Food is the everyday test of that prediction. Deng and colleagues catalogued the
food effect for 229 drugs and analysed it by BDDCS class
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40265-017-0832-z)), which turns "take with food"
from an instruction on a label into a statement about dissolution, gastric
emptying, bile salt solubilisation and splanchnic blood flow. For a modeller the
practical consequence is narrower: a fed–fasted difference is a *known
covariate on absorption*, and if your study allowed either, the dataset needs a
column for it.

## 3. Modality decides everything

"Drug" now covers wildly different kinds of matter. The differences are not
cosmetic — they change absorption, distribution, half-life, immunogenicity,
manufacturing, and every model you will build.

| Modality | Size | Typical route | Half-life | Cleared by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Small molecule** | 150–600 Da | Oral | Hours | Liver enzymes, kidney |
| **Peptide** | 1–5 kDa | Injection | Minutes–hours | Peptidases, kidney |
| **Monoclonal antibody** | ~150 kDa | IV or subcutaneous | **2–4 weeks** | Proteolysis; target binding |
| **Antibody–drug conjugate** | ~150 kDa + payload | IV | Days–weeks | Antibody plus payload routes |
| **Oligonucleotide** | 5–15 kDa | Injection | Days in plasma, **months in tissue** | Nucleases, kidney |
| **Cell therapy** (e.g. CAR-T) | Living cells | IV infusion | Cells *expand*, then persist for months–years | Immune contraction |
| **Gene therapy** | Viral vector | IV or local | Vector clears; effect may be permanent | — |

Three consequences worth carrying forward:

**Half-life spans six orders of magnitude.** A peptide may be gone in minutes; a
CAR-T product may still be detectable years later. "Once daily" is a small
molecule habit, not a law. The antibody figure is not an approximation for
teaching: elimination half-lives up to about four weeks are the reviewed norm,
and they arise because IgG bound by the neonatal Fc receptor is recycled rather
than degraded (Keizer et al., Clin Pharmacokinet 2010,
[DOI](https://doi.org/10.2165/11531280-000000000-00000); Liu, Protein Cell 2017,
[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13238-017-0408-4), free full text and **CC BY**).

**Big molecules cannot be swallowed.** They are digested, and they cannot cross
the gut wall. This alone determines route, and route determines the absorption
model.

**A cell therapy does not obey pharmacokinetics at all.** Cells *multiply*.
Concentration rises after dosing without any further dose, peaks days later, then
contracts. Every equation in `S1` assumes the amount of drug only ever goes down
between doses. For `CASE-CELL` that assumption is simply false, and the model has
to be rebuilt from the biology up — which is the whole point of `S4`.

The scale of the difference is worth seeing in numbers. The published
mixed-effects analysis of tisagenlecleucel reports a **doubling time of 0.78
days**, an initial decline half-life of **4.3 days**, and a terminal half-life of
**220 days** (Stein et al., CPT:PSP 2019,
[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12388), free full text) — expansion,
contraction and persistence as three distinct phases, none of them absorption or
elimination in the sense `S1` uses those words. A pooled analysis of 217 patients
across seven trials found that responders differed from non-responders in
proliferation rate and contraction rate, and that **dose was only weakly related
to exposure or to response** across the studied range (Liu et al., Clin Pharmacol
Ther 2021, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.2040), free full text). If your
instinct on reading that is "then what is the dose–response relationship for?",
you have located precisely why this modality needs its own model structure
rather than a reparameterised one.

## 4. What "drug-like" means

Most molecules that bind a target beautifully in a test tube never become
medicines. They fail on the journey, not on the target. Decades of attrition
produced rough empirical guidelines — famously the observation that orally
active drugs tend to be under ~500 Da, with limited hydrogen-bond donors and
acceptors and moderate lipophilicity.

These are **observations about what has historically worked orally**, not laws.
Plenty of important drugs violate them. But they capture a real tension that
never goes away:

> The properties that help a molecule cross membranes are broadly the same
> properties that make it insoluble, promiscuous and toxic.

Medicinal chemistry is the management of that trade-off. Modelling enters the
moment somebody asks *how much* of one property to trade for another — which is
exactly what a PBPK model (`S3`) is built to answer.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure mode — modelling a modality you have not understood
A team fits a standard two-compartment model to a monoclonal antibody and gets a
decent-looking fit at the doses studied. It then predicts badly at low doses.

The reason is biological, not statistical. Antibodies are cleared partly by
binding their own target, and that route **saturates**: at low concentrations a
large fraction of drug is consumed by target binding, at high concentrations that
route is swamped and clearance appears to fall. The result is nonlinear
pharmacokinetics that no linear model can represent, however good the fit looks
inside the observed range.

This is target-mediated drug disposition, and `S1` builds it properly. The
lesson here is the order of operations: **the biology chooses the model
structure.** A structure chosen for convenience will fit and then betray you at
the edges — which are exactly where you need predictions.

Two corrections worth carrying, both from the standard tutorial on the subject
(Dua, Hawkins & van der Graaf, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.41)). TMDD is
**not a biologics-only phenomenon** — the concept was introduced by Levy in 1994,
and the first drug described with it was *warfarin*, a small molecule. And TMDD
does **not automatically mean nonlinear pharmacokinetics**: where free target
concentration is negligible against free drug, a target-mediated compound can
show perfectly linear PK.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Why can you not simply swallow a monoclonal antibody?
Two independent reasons, either sufficient. It would be digested — an antibody
is a protein, and the gut exists to break proteins into amino acids. And even
intact, at ~150 kDa it is far too large to cross the intestinal wall, which
passes small, reasonably lipophilic molecules. This is why every marketed
antibody is injected, and why "oral biologics" remains a hard, largely unsolved
problem rather than a formulation detail.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. A drug is 95% absorbed from the gut but its oral bioavailability is 20%. Where did it go?
The liver, almost certainly. Blood leaving the gut goes to the liver before
reaching the rest of the body, so a well-absorbed drug can still have most of the
dose metabolised on that first pass. Absorption and bioavailability are different
quantities, and confusing them is a classic error: here absorption is excellent
and bioavailability is poor. Gut-wall metabolism can contribute too. `P-07`
separates the two properly.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Why does modality change the *sampling design* of a clinical study, not just the model?
Because sampling has to resolve the timescale of the process. A peptide with a
20-minute half-life needs samples every few minutes over a few hours; taking
them daily would show nothing but noise. An antibody with a three-week half-life
needs samples over months, and hourly sampling on day 1 wastes assay budget on a
curve that has barely moved. Design follows biology — which is why a modeller who
does not know the modality cannot design the study, and why the design question
usually arrives before any data exist.
:::

## Going further

- **Next:** [P-02 · Cells, proteins, and why molecules stick together](../p-02-cells-and-binding/)
- **Uses this:** every later strand. `S1` models small molecules and antibodies;
  `S3` needs the absorption story in detail; `S4` handles cells.
- **Reference:** Rang & Dale's *Pharmacology* for the broad tour; Rowland & Tozer
  for the quantitative version of this same journey.

*Seen in the wild:* the most expensive modality mistake is choosing one before
knowing where the target sits. An intracellular target rules out antibodies,
which cannot get into cells. That single fact has ended programmes after years of
work — and it is knowable on day one.
